messages.body_plain:
Thanks Steve,

If I’m understanding this correctly, I would complete many iterations of the comparison of the two abundances… using a R function like ‘nlnorm’ to simulate values of the two estimates, with D1 based on the field data estimate and with D2 being a reduction of D1 based on the effect size being tested (sd and df for both D1 and D2 based on the field data estimate). I would then look at the percentage of the comparisons that rejected the H0 to determine the power of the test in relation to the effect size and alpha value that was used.

I hope I’m correct as this seems to make sense.

Thanks again,

Mitch

Hi Eric,

sorry for the misunderstanding. You are right that the study area only concerns the western Baltic, the Belt Sea and the Kattegat. So the areas of interest from the German monitoring scheme actually are the strata I, J, K and L.

The idea was to use the existing strata (I, J, K and L) but just extend transects to cover a larger area. However, there are also several strata which have not existed before and thus need to be designed from scratch. I have attached a map of the currently planned strata. I is now extended northwards and called 'Kiel and Little Belt'. J and K ('Fehmarn' and 'Kadetrinne') have remained the same extent. L (here 'Rugen') has actually been extend towards the east (to meet the management border of this population) and there are no transects existing for this extension bit.

I guess the way forward you suggested is probably the best: Use a GIS system to extend the transects to the north for I, and also to create additional transects in regular spacing towards the east for L. Strata extent and transects for J and K will remain the same. I then need to assume two things: 1) that the coverage has been good for the existing strata and 2) will still be good for the new strata with my manual amendments. Concerning the first assumption I'm pretty confident it has been tested but concerning the second: is this fair to assume? Is there a way to check it?
For the new strata, however, I would then create a new design and assess coverage with dssd.

Best
Dominik

Victor

As I noted in my earlier reply, the inclusion of covariates in the detection function will provide some indication of whether detectability changes with the covariates included; it does not indicate whether primate abundance changes with the covariates.

Regarding your question about preference for detection function models 1) or 2).  My answer would be "neither".  The fitting of detection functions including covariates is more challenging than fitting detection functions without covariates.  To get a sense of this, I suggest you look at the lecture on covariates in the detection function here:
https://workshops.distancesampling.org/standrews-2019/intro/lectures/BlockH-covariates.pdf
As such, I have seldom encountered studies where more than 3-4 covariates are included in the modelling.  A property called "pooling robustness" ensures that (given g(0)=1), unbiased estimates of abundance are produced even if influential covariates are not included in the detection function model.

Your approach 2) is guaranteed to fail because there are too many covariates and consequently too many parameters to estimate.  Imagine each of your covariates has only two levels, that will result in (I think) an 8 parameter model.  Add more levels to the covariates and the number of parameters to estimate increases.  You will also encounter problems in data sparseness:  how many detections, across what range of detection distances will your data set have for month 1, location 1, animal 1, hactivity 1, logging 1, road 1 and Weather 1?  Likewise for all other covariate combinations.

Best to be very sparing in your use of covariates.  Look at scatterplots of detections or detection distances as functions of month, or logging, or road categories.  That should narrow the number of covariates you entertain for use in your models.

Eric Rexstad

On Friday, 24 April 2020 10:33:44 UTC+1, Eric Rexstad wrote:

> Leo
>
> Thanks for searching through the list; I don't think there is a general solution to this problem, because the introduction of covariates make even the question of detection probability challenging.  For example, you wish to know detection probability for each habitat type; that is an ambiguous question, because detection probability depends upon group size also.  So you must specify the value of group size for which you wish an estimate of habitat-specific detection probability.
>
> Computing detection probability requires integration of the detection function (with appropriate set of covariate coefficients) integrated over all perpendicular distances (out to w).  I'm not sure that code exists in a general setting for multiple covariates, but perhaps more clever folks will show I'm wrong.
>
> Rather than posing a solution to your detection probability estimates for various covariate combinations, I offer a mangled bit of code to draw pretty pictures of detection functions for combinations of a factor covariate with three levels and a continuous covariate of group size.  This approximates the scenario you described in your email.  I happen to have a data set for dolphins (provided with the Distance package) that I've tailored to suit our purposes.
>
> library(Distance)
> data(ETP_Dolphin)
> nohelio <- subset(ETP_Dolphin, ETP_Dolphin$Search.method != 3)
> luke <- ds(nohelio, key="hr", formula=~as.factor(Search.method)+log(size))
> plot.with.covariates <- function(dsobject, groupsize, plottitle) {
>   #   Purpose: plot detection function for each level of factor covariate
>   #   Input:   object of class ds produced by ds(),
>   #            fixed value of continuous group size covariate at which to evaluate detectability,
>   #            title for plot in quotes
>   #   Output:  plot
>   #   Author:  Rexstad, February 2020
>   #   Notes:   makes use of function detfct() to do the work.
>   stopifnot(class(dsobject)=="dsmodel",
>             is.character(plottitle))
>   myobject <- dsobject$ddf$ds$aux$ddfobj
>   truncation <- dsobject$ddf$meta.data$width
>   mycovariate <- myobject$xmat[,2]  # position in matrix when only a single covariate
>   thelevels <- unique(mycovariate)
>   covar.levels <- length(thelevels)
>   dists <- seq(from=0, to=truncation, length.out = 100)
>   xx <- matrix(data=NA, nrow=length(dists), ncol = covar.levels)
>   for (j in 1:covar.levels) {
>     this.dist <- 0
>     for (i in dists) {
>       this.dist <- this.dist + 1
>       tmpfilter <- myobject$xmat$size == groupsize & myobject$xmat[,2] == thelevels[j]
>       if (sum(tmpfilter) == 0) {
>         xx[this.dist, j] <- NA
>       } else {
>         xx[this.dist, j] <- unique(detfct(i, myobject, select=tmpfilter))
>       }
>     }
>   }
>
>   plot(dists, xx[,1], type='l', lty=1, ylim=c(0,1),
>        xlab="Distance (m)", ylab="Detection probability",
>        main=plottitle, sub=paste("For group size=", groupsize))
>   for (more.levels in 2:covar.levels) {
>     lines(dists, xx[,more.levels], type="l", lty=more.levels)
>   }
>   legend("topright", legend=attr(myobject$scale$dm, "dimnames")[[2]][1:covar.levels],
>          lty=seq(1:covar.levels), title="Covariate value")
> }
> plot.with.covariates(luke, 200, "example with dolphins")
> plot.with.covariates(luke, 300, "example with dolphins")

messages.body_plain:
Hi listfolk,

We've just uploaded mrds version 2.2.2 onto CRAN and it should now be
available for all platforms.

There are some changes that impact both mrds and Distance users, so I
thought I'd message the list to let you know.

The most obvious one is a change in plotting: following the release of R
4.0.0, there have been some changes to the default appearance of
histograms to have light grey bars. We've shifted to this too, so plots
look similar between R and mrds/Distance (this will also appear in the
next Distance for Windows release).

We've also added two new functions that we hope will help with your
analysis (examples of their use are available in their manual pages):

1. p_dist_table() prints a table of estimated probabilities of
detection. This is useful for covariate (MCDS) models to determine
issues with very small detectabilities (if estimated abundance seems
astronomically large, it may be down to one probability of detection
being very very small). This works for models fitted with mrds and Distance.

2. add_df_covar_line(), which can be used to add lines plots showing the
detection function for a given covariate combination. There have been
several requests for this over the years, so apologies that I've only
just got around to it. This works for models fitted with mrds and Distance.

You can see what's changed in the last few releases of mrds here:

https://cran.r-project.org/web/packages/mrds/NEWS

As usual, if you have issues please do report bugs either on github
(https://github.com/distancedevelopment/mrds/issues), to me or on this list.

Thanks,
--dave (on behalf of the Distance Development Team)

Sorry, I should have added that the values need to be normalized to
ensure that g(0)=1. You can do this by dividing your outp * adjterm by
the detection function evaluated at zero distance (x=0).

Looking back at your initial message, is it possible you have an extra
"/w" at the end of the line of code to calculate adjterm?

The following seems to give a reasonable result on my computer (based on
your code).

# set truncation
w <- 1100
# distances to evaluate at
x <- seq(0, 1100, length.out=2000)

# set parameters
sigma = exp(5.228683)
a2 <-  0.5019375
a3 <- -0.3270649
a4 <-  0.5232707

# key evaluation

outp = exp(- (x^2)/ (2*sigma^2))

# adjustment evaluation

adjterm = (1+ a2*cos(2*pi*x/w) + a3*cos(3*pi*x/w) + a4*cos(4*pi*x/w))

# detection function
g <- outp * adjterm

# g[1] = g(0)
plot(x, g/g[1])

cheers,
--dave

messages.body_plain:
I'm a long time (old time!) user of the software package Distance, but am attempting one of my first distance analyses in R and am struggling.

The data are from the Breeding Bird Survey, and are quite rudimentary in terms of the information they convey about distance. Two 'proper' (closed) distance bands of 0-25m and 25-100m, and a third band of >100m. After some thought we are treating this last category as a third closed band of 100-250m (we think this is reasonable for most of the species we are dealing with).

The surveys that generate the data are transects through a 1 km square. 2 x 1km transects are divided into a total of 10 x 200m sections, and the number of each species detected in each section/distance band combination is recorded. When more than one bird is recorded, we don't know whether these birds were seen together (i.e. a detection of a group) or separately. We have decided to treat each bird detected as a separate detection event (these are, for the most part, breeding waders, so they aren't in large groups and most detections will be of individual birds).

I've attached an example of an attempt at a flatfile format of data for analysis of one species (Curlew).

Each recorded bird gets its own row (as described above we are assuming all birds are detected independently of one another). The flatfile has the following columns.

Region.Label: In my full analysis I have specified several 'regions' each defined by a combination of period and whether the data derives from the Max Visit (the visit with the most observations) or the Min Visit (with the fewest). However, in the attached excerpt of example data I have included data from just one of these ‘regions’ (Max_Recent).

Sample.Label: This contains a unique identifier for every unique combination of square and ‘region’.

distance: The mid-point of the relevant distance band (i.e. 12.5, 62.5 or 175). In addition to a row for every bird recorded on the survey (with a valid entry in the 'distance' column), there is a 'blank' row (with NA in the distance column) for every survey carried out where no birds were detected. This is to make sure that surveys with no detections are taken into account.

Effort: Twice the total number of visits contributing data to the Sample.Label. Each survey visit comprises two 1km long transects.

Area: Because the Regions are actually periods, they each cover the entire survey area. Area is therefore the total land area of the UK, from which BBS squares are drawn.

The following code opens the relevant packages, sets up cutpoints, imports the data and runs the mode. The tic and toc commands, from package 'tictoc', return the time taken for the intervening code to run:

library (Distance)

library (tictoc)

Cuts <- c(0,025,100,250)

BBS_Example <- read.csv("Example_BBS_data.csv")

tic("Example_run")

CU_hn_example <- ds(BBS_Example, transect = "line", truncation = 250,cutpoints = Cuts)

toc()

summary(CU_hn_example)

When I run this, I get the following messages

Starting AIC adjustment term selection.

Fitting half-normal key function

Key only model: not constraining for monotonicity.

AIC= 15128.692

Fitting half-normal key function with cosine(2) adjustments

AIC= 15102.384

Fitting half-normal key function with cosine(2,3) adjustments

AIC= 15096.218

Fitting half-normal key function with cosine(2,3,4) adjustments

AIC= 15092.369

Fitting half-normal key function with cosine(2,3,4,5) adjustments

AIC= 15094.369

Half-normal key function with cosine(2,3,4) adjustments selected.

Error in t(partial) %*% vcov : non-conformable arguments

> toc()

Example_run: 302.67 sec elapsed

The distribution of observations between distance bands (see attached simple figure) looks sensible enough to me for a bird like Curlew, for which calls can be heard over 100s of metres. All units (relating to both area and distance) are in metres. Any advice would be hugely appreciated. Apologies if I've omitted any necessary information to diagnose this problem - please let me know and I'll provide whatever I can.

Hi Martin, hi listfolk,

The issue where I think is that "observer" is a reserved column name in
mrds (which powers Distance). Specifically observer is used to denote
which of the 2 observers an observation comes from when you're doing a
mark-recapture distance sampling survey.

Changing your column name to, say, "obs" should get you around this
problem for now. I'll add a check for this in Distance and some
additional documentation on these reserved column names.

Please do let me know if that doesn't fix things!

cheers,
--dave

This question is asked on the Distance list  on occasion.  Here is an answer I provided back in 2018:
> The answer is that the likelihood values are different according to the two different fitting engines.  The optimisation used to estimate the parameters of the hazard rate detection function are not the same, and for complex models, will produce slightly different estimates.  Because the hazard rate model is more complex than the half normal, the differences in the fitting algorithms are likely to be more pronounced with the hazard rate models.  This is a situation with which we are familiar and occurs in other data sets we have analysed.

The difference between results is exacerbated with the addition of the factor covariate.  Note particularly for the output from R the relative size of the point estimates and standard errors of the season factor covariates (suggesting the season effect is estimated imprecisely--there are only 5 detections in autumn).

There is nothing you have done wrong in your analysis.  However, the Distance for Windows output shows weak support for the presence of a season effect on detectability, consistent with the results from R.

messages.subject_clean: Distance sampling with camera traps - vignettes or training courses?
messages.body_plain:
Hi team,

Firstly thanks for the updated vignettes posted at https://examples.distancesampling.org/, I find these worked examples extremely useful to go from a theoretical description in a paper to the practical steps of an analysis.

So far I have used (thanks in large part to your support!) several variations of distance sampling, most recently cue counts for gibbons. We're now looking at methods for estimating density and abundance with camera traps for some low density species, specifically the approach described in Howe et al. 2018 (attached for those who are not familiar). The paper excellent, with a clear description of the method, and the data is also published which is great.

I was wondering if there were any plans to produce vignettes or training courses on this new method, or if a R Markdown file for the duiker analysis described in Howe et al was available?

Cheers,

Olly

On May 24 2020, at 11:10 pm, David Christianson <daveal...@gmail.com> wrote:

> Hello Eric,
> I have a more general questions about average detection probability (I am working in Jags, but the question is general).  I am fitting a half-normal detection function for line transect distance sampling.  If I wanted to calculate the average (or expected) detectability for any NEW individual in the population, is there a general approach for doing such a thing?  In my case the shape parameter (sigma) of the half normal is estimated using a linear model of the form log(sigma)<-log(sigma0) + alpha1*V1...
>
> My assumption has been that simply estimating the detection probability using the half-normal function for 100 distances from 0 out to the half strip width using the fitted sigma0 from the linear model (and averaging those probabilities) should do it, but I am uncertain.  My model for sigma includes other covariates but these are normally distributed (with mean 0).
>
>
> On Friday, April 24, 2020 at 3:33:44 AM UTC-6, Eric Rexstad wrote:
> > Leo
> >
> > Thanks for searching through the list; I don't think there is a general solution to this problem, because the introduction of covariates make even the question of detection probability challenging.  For example, you wish to know detection probability for each habitat type; that is an ambiguous question, because detection probability depends upon group size also.  So you must specify the value of group size for which you wish an estimate of habitat-specific detection probability.
> >
> > Computing detection probability requires integration of the detection function (with appropriate set of covariate coefficients) integrated over all perpendicular distances (out to w).  I'm not sure that code exists in a general setting for multiple covariates, but perhaps more clever folks will show I'm wrong.
> >
> > Rather than posing a solution to your detection probability estimates for various covariate combinations, I offer a mangled bit of code to draw pretty pictures of detection functions for combinations of a factor covariate with three levels and a continuous covariate of group size.  This approximates the scenario you described in your email.  I happen to have a data set for dolphins (provided with the Distance package) that I've tailored to suit our purposes.
> >
> > library(Distance)
> > data(ETP_Dolphin)
> > nohelio <- subset(ETP_Dolphin, ETP_Dolphin$Search.method != 3)
> > luke <- ds(nohelio, key="hr", formula=~as.factor(Search.method)+log(size))
> > plot.with.covariates <- function(dsobject, groupsize, plottitle) {
> >   #   Purpose: plot detection function for each level of factor covariate
> >   #   Input:   object of class ds produced by ds(),
> >   #            fixed value of continuous group size covariate at which to evaluate detectability,
> >   #            title for plot in quotes
> >   #   Output:  plot
> >   #   Author:  Rexstad, February 2020
> >   #   Notes:   makes use of function detfct() to do the work.
> >   stopifnot(class(dsobject)=="dsmodel",
> >             is.character(plottitle))
> >   myobject <- dsobject$ddf$ds$aux$ddfobj
> >   truncation <- dsobject$ddf$meta.data$width
> >   mycovariate <- myobject$xmat[,2]  # position in matrix when only a single covariate
> >   thelevels <- unique(mycovariate)
> >   covar.levels <- length(thelevels)
> >   dists <- seq(from=0, to=truncation, length.out = 100)
> >   xx <- matrix(data=NA, nrow=length(dists), ncol = covar.levels)
> >   for (j in 1:covar.levels) {
> >     this.dist <- 0
> >     for (i in dists) {
> >       this.dist <- this.dist + 1
> >       tmpfilter <- myobject$xmat$size == groupsize & myobject$xmat[,2] == thelevels[j]
> >       if (sum(tmpfilter) == 0) {
> >         xx[this.dist, j] <- NA
> >       } else {
> >         xx[this.dist, j] <- unique(detfct(i, myobject, select=tmpfilter))
> >       }
> >     }
> >   }
> >
> >   plot(dists, xx[,1], type='l', lty=1, ylim=c(0,1),
> >        xlab="Distance (m)", ylab="Detection probability",
> >        main=plottitle, sub=paste("For group size=", groupsize))
> >   for (more.levels in 2:covar.levels) {
> >     lines(dists, xx[,more.levels], type="l", lty=more.levels)
> >   }
> >   legend("topright", legend=attr(myobject$scale$dm, "dimnames")[[2]][1:covar.levels],
> >          lty=seq(1:covar.levels), title="Covariate value")
> > }
> > plot.with.covariates(luke, 200, "example with dolphins")
> > plot.with.covariates(luke, 300, "example with dolphins")
> >
> > Possibly this can either provide visual information to address your questions or provide some hints as to how to perform the computations you might require.
> >
> > Eric Rexstad
> > Senior Research Fellow, CREEM, Univ. of St Andrews, Charity SC013532
> > eric....@st-andrews.ac.uk
> > The Observatory, Buchanan Gardens, St Andrews KY16 9LZ
> > On Apr 23 2020, at 6:36 pm, Leo Lamb <leol...@gmail.com> wrote:
> > > Hi everyone,
> > >
> > > I have been trying to find an answer to my question in the google group but forgive me if I missed it.
> > > I am analysing line transect data and incorporating a group size adjustment plus a habitat covariate.
> > > My output looks like this:
> > >
> > > Detection function parameters
> > > Scale coefficient(s):
> > >               estimate         se
> > > (Intercept) -3.0625682 0.08726965
> > > gstageopen   0.6781189 0.13301283
> > > gstagethick -0.1887549 0.06083695

> > >

> > > Instead of getting average p, I would like to get p for each of my habitat type. I understand that the detectability is lower in my thick forest and higher in the open than it is in my reference category (mature), but I don't really know how to use these scale coefficients to get to p.
